description.summary: An anonymous online persona who, between 1998 and 2001, claimed to be an American soldier from the year 2036 sent back to 1975 to retrieve an IBM 5100 computer. Widely regarded as one of the most elaborate early-internet hoaxes.
description.full: John Titor is the screen name attached to a series of online posts claiming time-traveler status that appeared on the Art Bell Post-2-Post BBS, Time Travel Institute forums, and IRC channels between 1998 and late March 2001. The earliest known communications were two faxes sent to broadcaster Art Bell on 29 July 1998. The poster claimed to be a US Army soldier born in 1998 and based in Tampa, Florida in 2036, sent back to 1975 to retrieve an IBM 5100 computer needed to debug legacy systems threatened by the year-2038 Unix problem ('Y2038'); he claimed to be 'on a stopover' in 2000-2001 to visit his family. He posted detailed schematics, photographs of an alleged 'time displacement device' built into a 1967 Chevrolet Corvette and 1987 truck, and a series of predictions including civil unrest around the 2004 US presidential election, a US civil war by 2008, and a global nuclear war ('N-Day') in 2015 with the new US capital relocated to Omaha, Nebraska. None of the predictions came to pass on schedule. A 2009 investigation by John Hughston ('Razimus') and Italian researchers identified Larry Haber, a Florida entertainment lawyer who became CEO of the John Titor Foundation (incorporated 2003-09-16), as the most likely originator, alongside his brothers Morey Haber and John Rick Haber - all of whom have denied involvement. The Titor archive remains one of the most enduring artifacts of late-1990s/early-2000s internet folklore.

etymology.origin: The pseudonym 'John Titor' was used on the Art Bell BBS forum from January 2001; earlier posts on the Time Travel Institute used 'TimeTravel_0'. The name 'Titor' has no announced derivation in the original posts.
etymology.first_use: 1998-07-29 (two faxes to Art Bell, signed as a time traveler) / 2000-11-02 (first Time Travel Institute post as 'TimeTravel_0')

related_phenomena.name: Mandela Effect
related_phenomena.description: Internet-era memory anomaly often grouped with parallel-universe claims

physical.morphology: Phenomenon is textual/online; no physical form.

abilities.ability: Claimed time travel via 'time displacement unit'
abilities.description: Titor described a device installed in a 1967 Chevrolet Corvette (and later a 1987 truck) using two micro-singularities and a magnetic-field manipulation system

patterns: Detailed pseudo-technical posts about time-machine engineering
Specific dated predictions about US politics, war, and the Y2038 problem

range.description: Posts originated through online forums based primarily in the United States.

origins.cultural_roots: Late-1990s American conspiracy/paranormal radio (Coast to Coast AM with Art Bell), early-internet bulletin-board culture, and Y2K/Y2038 anxiety.
origins.earliest_accounts: Two faxes to Art Bell on 29 July 1998 from someone identifying as a time traveler.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to broader American time-travel legends (Philadelphia Experiment, Montauk Project) and to internet creepypasta traditions that succeeded it.

history.modern_era: The Titor archive endures as a foundational text of internet folklore, regularly cited in retrospectives and analyzed in academic studies of online hoaxes (e.g. Brian Dunning's Skeptoid, Jenny Kleeman, The New Republic). The case is widely treated by mainstream commentators as a hoax.

notable.name: Art Bell time-traveler faxes

location.description: Art Bell's broadcast/fax line, Pahrump, Nevada

credibility_factors: Bell preserved and discussed the faxes on air

notable.description: Art Bell received two faxes from a person claiming to be a time traveler. These are the earliest known communications later linked to the John Titor persona.

notable.name: First TimeTravel_0 post
notable.description: First public forum post under the username 'TimeTravel_0', launching what would become the John Titor narrative.

credibility.notes: Beginning of the main online phase.

photographic.name: Alleged 1967 Chevrolet Corvette 'time machine' photographs
photographic.description: Photographs and schematics posted by Titor of an alleged 'time displacement unit' installed in a 1967 Chevrolet Corvette and a 1987 truck.
photographic.analysis: Mainstream commentators treat the schematics as pseudo-technical fiction; the photographs have not been authenticated.

documentary.name: John Titor forum archive
documentary.description: Compiled archive of Titor's posts on the Time Travel Institute and Art Bell BBS, mirrored in many third-party locations.
documentary.analysis: All major predictions falsified; credible attribution to the Haber brothers stands unrefuted.

paranormal.name: Genuine time traveler from 2036
paranormal.description: Titor's own claim: an American soldier sent back from 2036 via a micro-singularity-based time-displacement unit to retrieve an IBM 5100 computer for the Y2038 problem.

paranormal.name: Alternate-history Titor
paranormal.description: A defense sometimes raised after predictions failed: Titor came from a divergent timeline and his future is not ours.
evidence_cited: Titor's own statements about a roughly 2.5% divergence between worldlines

skeptical.name: Larry Haber / Haber brothers hoax
skeptical.description: The most credible attribution: Florida entertainment lawyer Larry Haber, who became CEO of the John Titor Foundation Inc. (incorporated 16 September 2003), and/or his computer-professional brothers Morey Haber and John Rick Haber, originated the Titor posts. All deny involvement.
evidence_cited: Commercial development of Titor IP through the foundation

skeptical.name: Falsified predictions
skeptical.description: Titor's central predictions - civil unrest in 2004, US civil war by 2008, global nuclear war ('N-Day') in 2015 - did not occur.
evidence_cited: Continuing existence of Washington, D.C. as US capital

skeptical.name: Internet-folklore hoax tradition
skeptical.description: Titor fits a recognizable pattern of late-1990s/early-2000s internet hoaxes (alongside earlier and later examples), exploiting the credibility of forum culture and Art Bell's audience.
evidence_cited: Stylistic similarity to other forum hoaxes

traditions: Coast to Coast AM paranormal radio tradition

stories: The Y2038 mission: retrieving an IBM 5100 from 1975

folklore.beliefs: Treated by mainstream commentators and journalists as a hoax; small online communities continue to defend the alternate-timeline reading.
